title: Despite $120,000 Job Offer, NRI Wants To Return To India: 'I Am Too Depressed'
excerpt: A viral social media post reignites the debate about mental health, loneliness, and the hidden costs of the NRI dream as more Indians abroad weigh returning home.
body:
• An NRI earning $120,000 in the US shared a post saying they want to return to India despite the financial sacrifice, citing depression and isolation.
  • The post went viral on social media, drawing thousands of comments from Indians abroad sharing similar struggles with loneliness and mental health.
  • Reverse migration to India is growing, driven by improving domestic salaries, family ties, and quality-of-life concerns that salary alone cannot address.
  • Mental health experts say the NRI experience carries unique stressors including cultural isolation, visa anxiety, and the pressure to justify the decision to emigrate.

When the Salary Isn't Enough

A post from an Indian professional in the United States has gone viral after they publicly questioned whether a $120,000 salary is worth the depression and loneliness that comes with living abroad. Writing on social media, the individual described feelings of deep isolation, cultural disconnection, and a persistent sadness that the financial comforts of an American life could not address.

"I am too depressed," the post read. "Some days I just sit in my apartment and wonder what the point of all this is. I have money, I have a job, but I have no life."

"I have money, I have a job, but I have no life."</p> <p>The confession struck a nerve."

The confession struck a nerve. Within days, it accumulated thousands of comments and shares from Indians across the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, and the Gulf, many echoing the same sentiment: financial success abroad does not guarantee happiness, and the emotional cost of the NRI dream is rarely discussed before the plane ticket is booked.

The Loneliness Epidemic Among NRIs

Mental health professionals who work with South Asian communities say the post reflects a broader, underreported crisis. The NRI experience carries a unique set of stressors: cultural isolation in countries where social networks are built around different norms, constant visa anxiety for those on H-1B or other temporary work permits, the guilt of being away from aging parents, and the unspoken pressure to justify the decision to emigrate by appearing successful.

"There is an enormous gap between the life NRIs project on social media and the loneliness many experience behind closed doors."

— Mental Health Professional Working With South Asian Communities

The problem is compounded by cultural stigma around mental health in Indian communities. Seeking therapy is still viewed with suspicion in many families, and the narrative of the successful NRI leaves little room for admitting struggle.

Reverse Migration Is Growing

The post also reignited discussion about reverse migration — Indians who have built careers abroad choosing to return home. India's technology sector now offers salaries that, adjusted for cost of living, rival mid-tier US compensation. Bengaluru, Hyderabad, and Pune have emerged as genuine alternatives for tech professionals, with the added benefit of family proximity, cultural familiarity, and a social life that doesn't need to be built from scratch.

Data from LinkedIn and recruitment firms show a steady increase in Indian professionals exploring return options, particularly since the pandemic normalized remote work and exposed the vulnerability of visa-dependent life. The H-1B uncertainty under successive US administrations has further accelerated the trend.

What's Next

The conversation the post has sparked is valuable precisely because it challenges the one-dimensional narrative of NRI success. For Indians considering the move abroad, it's a reminder that salary is one variable in a complex equation that includes mental health, community, family, and purpose. For those already abroad and struggling, the thousands of similar comments offer something equally important: the knowledge that they're not alone.
nri_angle: Directly addresses the NRI experience of loneliness and mental health challenges, a core concern for the diaspora audience.
